Literature:
Anna Koopstra & Luuk Hoogsteded, "Observaties over de werkwijze van Lucas Gassel," Lucas Gassel van Helmond: Meester van het landschap, Zwolle, 2020, exh. cat., pp. 50-51, fig. 13, illus.

Lot Essay:
Comparatively little is known of Lucas Gassel’s life. He was probably born circa 1488 in Deurne, a well-to-do municipality east of Antwerp, to the painter Jan Thonisz. van Gassel. It is assumed that Lucas left for Antwerp at the turn of the sixteenth century, which at that time, was an important city for the arts. Gassel later moved to Brussels, where he remained until his death. A successful painter and artist in the sixteenth century, Gassel’s small oeuvre, includes some fifteen signed and dated paintings, all in oil on wooden panels; two drawings that are signed and dated; and three prints that have an LG monogram. He is one of only a handful of artists whose names are known as early practitioners of the landscape genre, together with Joachim Patinir (ca. 1480-1524) and Herri met de Bles (ca. 1510-ca-15510). Gassel’s portrait is known in a print by Jacob Binck, dated 1529, nine years before the artist’s known earliest dated work, which shows that he was by then already well-to-do.

The present panel painting, monogrammed and dated 1541, is an example of a composition of which Gassel did several versions that depict Abraham and the Angels. As is typical for the artist, the overall composition is ‘closed off’ with trees and foliage, which act as repoussoir elements, a common feature of Gassel’s works. The color palette of the painting is characterized by earthy brown and green tones that are stronger in the foreground and become paler and lighter into the distance, with the pale light sky as its culmination. In the center, placed below the foreground to establish perspective, the small figures of Abraham and the three angels, one of which was God, can be seen, with Abraham offering the angels hospitality, who then in turn revealed to Abraham that his elderly wife Sarah was to have a son within a year. Behind this figural group, to the right and left, are typical 16th century Flemish buildings, along with a somewhat fanciful fountain, and scattered figures going about their daily business. A verdant slope climbs up from this middle ground to a rocky escarpment extends into the upper right corner, further establishing depth.

Occupying this escarpment is a castle-like structure, which is likely meant to represent Somom and Gomorrah, as miniature fires and smoke can be seen amongst the fortifications. In the lower right corner, Abraham kneels in front of the angels, pleading with them to spare the inhabitants of Somom and Gomorrah, so that at least the righteous of those towns can survive. According to Dr. Anna Koopstra, these may not be autograph figures. (A. Koopstra, Lucas Gassel van Helmond. Meester van het landschap, Zwolle, 2020, exhib. cat., p. 52) It is possible that Gassel’s workshop may have produced these figures, but this cannot be determined without additional imaging at this time.

Lot Essay:
Comparatively little is known of Lucas Gassel’s life. He was probably born circa 1488 in Deurne, a well-to-do municipality east of Antwerp, to the painter Jan Thonisz. van Gassel. It is assumed that Lucas left for Antwerp at the turn of the sixteenth century, which at that time, was an important city for the arts. Gassel later moved to Brussels, where he remained until his death. A successful painter and artist in the sixteenth century, Gassel’s small oeuvre, includes some fifteen signed and dated paintings, all in oil on wooden panels; two drawings that are signed and dated; and three prints that have an LG monogram. He is one of only a handful of artists whose names are known as early practitioners of the landscape genre, together with Joachim Patinir (ca. 1480-1524) and Herri met de Bles (ca. 1510-ca-1510). Gassel’s portrait is known in a print by Jacob Binck, dated 1529, nine years before the artist’s known earliest dated work, which shows that he was by then already well-to-do.

The present panel painting, dated to 1542, has until now been completely unknown or published before, as it has been in private collections since at least 1949. The work depicts the baptism of Christ by John the Baptist in the river Jordan. They are surrounded by large rocky formations, with the dove of the Holy Spirit present, and at the top of the panel, God the Father hovering in the sky. In the left background, Jesus Christ is shown preaching underneath the trees to a small crowd. In the right foreground, the Jewish Pharisee and Sadducee leaders witness the baptism, identified by the Hebrew-like text on their headgear. In the background, a winding road leads the eye into the distance, via a rolling landscape with an assortment of houses and a church. The diagonals that govern the composition add to the scene’s dynamic movement. To the right and left, the composition is ‘closed off’ with trees and foliage. These act as repoussoir elements, a common feature of Gassel’s works, and together with the rocky plateaus establish depth. The color palette of the painting is characterized by earthy brown and green tones that are stronger in the foreground and become paler and lighter into the distance, with the pale light sky as its culmination. This use of color to establish perspective is typical for the artist. Additionally, infrared photography reveals the composition is fully underdrawn, a distinctive feature of Gassel’s works, and the free style and approach is very comparable to that in other underdrawings in the artist’s core works (For the most recent publication on Gassel’s life and oeuvre see Anna Koopstra, Lucas Gassel van Helmond. Meester van het landschap, 2020, published in conjunction with the exhibition of the same title, shown at Museum Helmond).

Prior to the discovery of the present work, the only known painting by Gassel with the same subject, also signed and dated to 1542, was formerly in the collection of Fernand Stuyck in Antwerp (current location unknown). The composition of the former Stucyk painting is typical of the artist, with elements like the centrally placed main figures, the view into the distance, and on each side smaller auxiliary scenes. Furthermore, the composition was extensively underdrawn, in a free manner that shows numerous changes. In comparison to the former Stuyck Baptism of Christ, in the present painting, the group of onlookers and episode of Christ preaching have been switched from left to right, with the signature and date placed near them for optimal visibility, and the owl conspicuously located on the left.

One of Gassel’s best and most characteristic paintings in terms of materials and approach, the Flight on the way to Egypt (on loan from the Cultural Heritage Agency of the Netherlands to Bonnefantenmuseum, Maastricht), is also dated 1542 and signed with the letters LG. The dimensions of the panel in Maastricht, which consists of three horizontally joined planks, 71.2 x 91.1 cm, occur in more than one work, and are close to the present panel, indicating this may have been a favored format of the artist and/or his panelmaker who supplied him with the wooden supports to paint on.

While Gassel’s oeuvre appears small and consistent in working methods, style and approach, the artist’s workshop produced works of slightly lesser quality and with evident involvement of different hands in the painting stage. This is already the case for the Maastricht Flight on the way to Egypt of 1542, of which at least three contemporary versions exist, that were probably made after the finished original, which makes it hard to establish whether they were produced within Gassel’s workshop or not. Another composition of which there is more than one version is the signed Abraham meeting the Angels, 1541. Thus, it is possible that already in the early 1540s Gassel’s own workshop produced the same compositions, in small numbers.

In the present Baptism of Christ, the scale of the small main protagonists in relation to the group of onlookers to the right is unusual for the artist. The figures themselves are also stylistically different from those seen in other signed and dated works by Gassel, which suggests the involvement of the workshop is possible. Also uncommon, iconographically as well as formally, is that the river Jordan does not continue but instead is replaced mid-composition by a view of a road into the village. This does not occur in any of the other compositions of the baptism of Christ related to Gassel.

Curious as well is the prominently placed owl, which does not feature regularly in the artist’s oeuvre, although an owl does occur in Gassel’s painting in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, a 1548 landscape with Tamar and Judah. Owls were, however, often included in works by Gassel’s contemporary, Herri Met de Bles. In a 1659 inventory of the collection of Archduke Leopold Wilhelm, the painting in the Kunsthistorisches Museum was erroneously attributed to Met de Bles. This artist’s work was popular in Italy, and he was referred to in that country as Civetta, Italian for little owl. A modern inscription on the back of the frame on the present panel indeed mentions Met de Bles (as Civetta), confirming its recent whereabouts in Italy. It is possible that the owl was included deliberately because the painting was made for export to Italy, which aligns with the work’s provenance.

Lot Essay:
Italianate River Landscape with Witches Sacrifice and Castle Ruins in a Distance is one of only approximately 70 or so paintings known by Moses van Uyttenbroeck, a relatively rare Dutch artist active in the Hague in the second quarter of the 17th century. He entered the city's painters guild in 1620, and specialized in sweeping Italianate landscapes often animated with historical or mythological subjects. The present example, with the figures confined to the lower right corner, is stylistically similar to other works by Uyttenbroeck from the 1620s, where influence of artists such as Bartholomeus Breenbergh (Dutch, 1598-1657) and Cornelis Van Poelenburgh (Dutch, 1586-1667) are visible.

Within a vast river landscape, three witches tend to the flames of a sacrificial pyre set before a stone statue. Two men in classical attire kneel before the women to present a pile of timber for the fire. To the group’s left, castle ruins loom in the distance. This as-yet unidentified subject may have mythological roots. It may also have its origins in Ovid's Metamorphoses, such as Medea's sacrifices (Book VII), although it does not conform to any specific passage. Other possible sources of visual inspiration may likewise be found in Jacques de Gheyn II's drawings and prints of witchcraft, including one such example, Witches’ Sabbath, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. De Gheyn II completed many such works between 1600-1610 while living in The Hague, where Uyttenbroeck lived and worked all his life.

In his 1964 Oud Hollande article, “The Paintings of Moses van Wtenbrouck,” art historian Ulrich Weisner was the first to surmise that this painting may be the one listed in the estate inventory of the artist's daughter, Cornelia van Uyttenbroeck, as Een heydense offerande, or as translated, A pagan offering. However, as many Pre-Rembrandtist history paintings are recorded with this title in inventories and auction catalogues, the identification of the painting in Cornelia's collection may never be fully certain.

artwork_title: A Wooded Landscape with Horse-Drawn Wagons
provenance:
The present lot was authenticated by Dr. Klaus Ertz when previously offered at action, and accompanied with a certificate of authenticity dated December 13, 1994.

Provenance:
Sotheby's, New York, sale of January 31, 1997, lot 8 (as A Wooden Landscape with Horse-Drawn Carts, Riders and Peasants on a Hillside Path in the Foreground, where listed as indistinctly signed Brueghel).
Acquired directly from the above sale by the present owner.

Lot Essay:
Jan Brueghel the Younger was born into a dynasty of painters that began with Pieter Bruegel the Elder, and continuing to his sons, Pieter Brueghel the Younger and Jan Brueghel the Elder. While some of Jan Brueghel the Younger’s paintings show the influence of his father’s work (he is known at times to have copied his father’s paintings and for adding his father’s signature to his own works) Jan the Younger was a highly skilled painter in his own right, taking over his father’s studio in Antwerp and becoming the dean of that city’s guild in 1630.

The present painting is a superb example of the son’s ability to depict an everyday scene – a panoramic landscape with horse carts and travelers from a slightly elevated perspective, in which the viewer is invited to enter the picture at left. The composition is well-staged with the rider in the horse cart in the foreground, the second horse cart in the midground, and the descending line of trees that draws the viewer to the lower center right, with the jumping dog and traveler on horseback directly behind, along with the line of figures in the distance, which draws the viewer’s eye back again from right to left. Brueghel the Younger’s brushwork is meticulously applied with no detail spared, so the viewer is treated to his rendering of individual grasses on the hill at left, feathery tree leaves, remnants of an animal skull, a single bird at lower center, and even a distant village at center right. The coloration of this painting is also noteworthy, with the rider’s vibrant red shirt effectively contrasted against the soft greens and browns of the landscape and pale blue sky.

artist_name: Follower of Melchior de Hondecoeter (1636-1695) | Attributed to Philips van Kouwenberg (1671-1729)
provenance:
We would like to thank Mr. Fred Meijer for his kind assistance in researching and cataloguing the present lot.

Provenance:
Purchased by the City of Philadelphia with the W. P. Wilstach Fund, Philadelphia, November 30, 1896 (as 'Workshop of Melchior de Hondecoeter' (Dutch, 1636-1695)).
Collection of the Philadelphia Museum of Art (now Philadelphia Art Museum), Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (accession number W1896-1-12).

Lot Note:
This large and lively Poultry Yard reflects the enduring popularity of Melchior d’Hondecoeter’s bird scenes, and ultimately set the standard for Dutch animal painting in the late seventeenth century. The subject, featuring a peacock, rooster, and an assortment of domestic and exotic fowl animated before a formal garden, derives closely from a smaller, more refined version in the Hamburger Kunsthalle (Revolt in the Poultry Coop) and from several other known variants inventoried through the RKD. 

The Philadelphia painting however, is significantly enlarged along the left and lower edges. Differences in handling between the central birds (most notably the meticulously rendered peacock and rooster) and those on the periphery suggest multiple hands at work, thus making it a collaborative work, or at least a composition executed in a workshop setting. In 1990, correspondence between the Philadelphia Museum of Art and Professor Fred Meijer in the Netherlands suggested the lavish bouquet and surrounding vegetation were in fact painted by Philip van Kouwenbergh (1671–1729), an artist celebrated for his floral still lifes who often borrowed motifs from d’Hondecoeter’s compositions. Indeed, the floral passage and certain landscape elements appear consistent with Kouwenbergh’s style, while many of the bird motifs repeat known Hondecoeter models—including the cluster of chicks in the foreground, directly echoing Seven Chicks, a workshop study now in the Rijksmuseum.

Whether Kouwenbergh collaborated with a follower of Hondecoeter or executed the entire composition within his own studio remains uncertain. The painting nonetheless illustrates the diffusion of Hondecoeter’s imagery in the decades following his death, as later painters adapted and expanded his celebrated poultry-yard scenes for a new generation of collectors.

artwork_title: Tabletop Still Life with Lobster, Lemons, Grapes, a Lute, and Tankards
provenance:
We would like to thank Mr. Fred Meijer for his kind assistance in researching and cataloguing the present lot.

Provenance:
Newman Galleries, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
Collection of Marguerite Harris Morrison (1912-2003), Media, Pennsylvania.
Bequeathed from the above in 2003 (as 'Jan Pauwel Gillemans').
Collection of the Philadelphia Museum of Art (Now Philadelphia Art Museum), Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (never officially accessioned).

Lot Note:
This sumptuous still life, with its lobster, gleaming silverware, and scattered musical instruments, epitomizes the opulent pronkstilleven tradition developed in Antwerp during the mid-seventeenth century. The painting was long attributed to Jan Pauwel Gillemans due to its close resemblance to other Gillemans’s known works, such as the Großes Stilleben in the Museum der Bildenden Künste, Leipzig, and the very similar composition sold at Christie’s in 2012 (Pronk Still Life with Fruit and a Lobster, Christie’s London, 3–4 July 2012, lot 152), further contributed to this attribution.

Recent scholarship led by Professor Fred Meijer, however, considers the signature and date spurious and instead supports a reattribution to Andries de Coninck, an Antwerp still-life painter active between 1643 and 1659, whose work was deeply indebted to Jan Davidsz. de Heem. According to Professor Meijer, de Coninck was among the first Antwerp painters to translate de Heem’s large and luxurious still lifes of the early 1640s into more intimate yet densely arranged compositions, as seen here. The present lot clearly adopts the artist’s characteristic restrained palette and compositional device centered around the eye-catching lobster perched atop a wicker basket, echoing the soft illumination of the surrounding fruit and glass, and adding to the sense of quiet grandeur set by the classical architectural backdrop. The painting also reveals de Coninck’s fascination with the sensuous tactility of objects: the gleaming goblet half-filled with wine, the curling sheet of music beside the lute, and the cascade of grapes and lemons spilling toward the viewer. 

Yet amid this splendor, the overturned glass, the drooping vine, and the fading light betray a meditation on the fleeting nature of pleasure and possession. In its union of opulence and transience, the painting transforms luxury into allegory: a banquet poised on the edge of silence, where abundance itself becomes a reminder of time’s inevitable decay.

Giovanni Paolo Panini was born in Piacenza and received his early training in the studio of Bolognese stage designers. After moving to Rome by 1711, he studied briefly with Benedetto Luti. Panini specialized in capricci of Roman ruins and in recording events of historical significance, though it is the former for which he is best known. Of these, some are accurate topographical records (vedute reale) while others are all or in part imaginary, composed perhaps as a pastiche of real views (vedute ideale). This genre of painting, with a primary focus on classical ruins, was known as Rovinismo, and was practiced by a sizeable group of painters including Bartholomeus Breenbergh, Viviano Codazzi, and Giovanni Ghisolfi. In 1732, Panini was elected a member of the French Academy in Rome, where he taught classes in optics and perspective.

Literature:

Lot Essay:
The Invention of Painting is a relatively recent rediscovery. Originally sold anonymously in a European salesroom as a work by Tischbein, it was later reattributed to Jean Raoux and exhibited at the Musée Fabre in the artist’s native Montpellier from November 2009 to March 2010. The exhibition, titled Virtuose et sensuel, paid homage to the lyrical grace, warm tonality, and masterful interplay of light and shadow that characterize this Peintre sous la Régence.

Often considered the pendant to Raoux’s Pygmalion Amoureux de sa Statue (the work that secured his admission to the Académie and which illustrated the birth of sculpture), The Invention of Painting illustrates the myth of Dibutade, guided by Cupid’s torch as she traces the outline of her lover’s shadow. According to the legend, Dibutade, the daughter of a sculptor from Corinth, wished to preserve the image of her beloved as he set out for a distant voyage, and drew the outline of his shadow on the wall; her father then filled the traced form with clay, thus creating the first sculpted portrait. In both works, love itself becomes the animating force, the divine spark that inspires creation, a notion central to artistic theory since the Renaissance.

Belonging successively to three distinguished collectors, The Invention of Painting exemplifies Jean Raoux’s inimitable style, instantly recognizable in the woman’s golden hair and that of her lover, rendered with the same refined sensuality found in his celebrated Pygmalion,. The painting displays Raoux’s exceptional command of light and shadow and his judicious attention to detail: the archer’s quiver, the giltwood chair, and the faithful dog—all few in number yet executed with exquisite precision, each contributing meaningfully to the narrative. 

In this composition, Cupid stands at left, balancing against a column while holding a torch that illuminates the scene from left to right, casting a shadow behind Dibutade’s lover draped in Graeco-Roman attire. His silhouetted outline is carefully traced by Dibutade herself, similarly dressed, who kneels gracefully upon a velvet-covered bench, steadying herself with one hand on the man’s arm. As the viewer witnesses Raoux’s poetic vision of the birth of painting, a small dog in the lower left corner looks upward toward Cupid, subtly anchoring the scene in domestic intimacy.

Trained first under Jean Ranc and later as a pupil of Bon de Boullogne, Raoux traveled to Italy to study the great masters before returning to France, where he distinguished himself among patrons as a painter of elegant figures, softened forms, and diffused light. The inclusion of the small dog in the present work recalls the Venetian compositions the artist would have studied during his Italian sojourn and has led scholars to situate the present work either during Raoux’s stay in Italy or shortly after his return to Paris, around 1714-1717.

Literature:

Lot Essay:
Well known and highly regarded as a painter of Mediterranean marine capriccios, nocturnes, harbor scenes, and port views, with fisherfolk and merchants depicted along the shoreline or in shallow waters dwarfed by resplendent vistas, scenes of Mount Vesuvius erupting at nighttime are known to have been painted by Lacroix in the 1750s. These views occupy a somewhat small but important component of his work and are a subject that was not widely treated by Claude-Joseph Vernet, with whom Lacroix's work is most frequently associated and who is generally believed to have been the artist's greatest influence.

While not a great deal is known about Lacroix, he excelled in capturing the effects of light, shadow, and color, evident in the present painting with the volcano's orange hue glowing across the water and the masted ship at right emerging from a break in the otherwise darkened skies. While there is a certain stillness in his Vesuvius compositions - witness the calm and gentle ripples in the water - there is also an understated sublime quality present. The group of fishermen, each presented leaning left to right created a slight sense of movement and makes for an interesting compositional contrast with the verticality of the rest of the painting.

Lot Essay:
In this rare pair of paintings by Francesco Zugno the Younger, the artist can be seen combining Old Testament stories with a sense of delicacy, elegance, pastel palette, and eighteenth-century fashion, all of which characterizes Italian Rococo art. One of its greatest practitioners was the famed Venetian artist, Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, in whose workshop Zugno entered in 1730 and with whom he worked. Perhaps it is therefore not surprising that in 1920 when in the collection of The 2nd. Lord Alington, the present pair were believed to be by Tiepolo himself. In fact, Tiepolo painted these very subjects: Laban looking for Idols (Palazzo Patriarcale, Venice) and The Finding of Moses (Scottish National Gallery, Edinburgh).

In Zugno's paintings, the various figures are treated in a somewhat fanciful manner while maintaining fidelity to the stories, with Rachel seated on her camel's saddle, concealing the idols (teraphim) she has stolen from her father Laban, and with Moses being discovered by the Pharaoh's daughter, saving the child who was hidden by his mother in the bulrushes near the Nile River.

Lot Essay:
Portrait of Nikolai Alekseevich Stolypin, 1849, is fascinating work that represents both 19th century artistic cross-cultural currents and the work of woman artist who was famous during her time but now little known. Christina Robertson was born in 1796 in Kinghorn, Scotland, and was possibly trained by her London-based uncle, George Sa(u)nders. She quickly established a reputation as portrait and miniature painter, with a flow of commissions from Scottish patrons. By 1823, she had married the artist James Robertson, whose own career was soon to be eclipsed by his wife’s. In 1828, Robertson had her own studio and the following year, she became the first honorary woman member of the Royal Scottish Academy.

After the birth of her eighth child (four children lived past infancy), the artist traveled to France to broaden her career. During a length stay in Paris starting in 1835, she painted a number of notables, including various members of St. Petersburg society that were resident there. In 1839, Robertson made the journey to Russia, likely encouraged by the positive reactions her Paris portraits of Russian nobility. She was at the height of her popularity at this time, in part due to engravings that were made after her paintings, which appeared in numerous illustrated lady’s journals and albums of the 1830s and 1840s that circulated both at home and abroad. Several volumes of Heath’s Book of Beauty, for instance, once belonged to Empress Alexandra Fyodorovna, wife of Nicholas I.

Robertson was very well received at the Russian court of Tsar Nicholas I and his empress, which at the time was gripped by Anglomania. The British artist’s ability to match current fashionable trends, paired with her depictions of delicate, elegant female images, were just what was wanted at the Russian court. From 1839 to 1841, Robertson was in St. Petersburg, where she carried out full-length portraits of Tsar Nicholas I and Empress Alexandra and her three daughters, Maria, Olga, and Alexandria. In his review of the 1839 exhibition at the Imperial Academy of Arts in St. Petersburg, the critic Pavel Kamensky wrote that Robertson’s portrait of Maria Kochubey, née Baryatinskaya, was the best portrait of all those shown:

This might confidently be placed alongside Rembrandt, and it would lose little from such a dangerous comparison. What a bold, powerful brush! How all is simple, natural what superb colouring! And who would have thought? All this is the work of a weak woman’s hand! Or, more correctly, only a woman could paint this: a man would not be capable of so much feeling... It is immediately clear that Mrs Robertson is an Englishwoman [sic], that she was brought up in the traditions of sublime portrait painting, that she studied mastery of the brush in the land of Reynolds and Lawrence. (P. P. Kamensky, Exhibition of Russian Works of Art in St Petersburg and Rome 1839, Readers’ Library, vol. 37, 1839, section II, pp. 53-54)

In 1841, she was the first, and only woman, to be made an honorary member, of the Imperial Academy of Arts. The same year, Robertson returned to her family and home in London in 1841, where she worked until her second visit to Russia, from 1847 to 1854. She found success again with Russia’s noble families, presenting society beauties in their best light. Her skillful depictions include the women’s fashionable garments, luxurious gold bracelets, and shining pearls, as well as other opulent accessories, such as vases, candelabra, and especially flowers, dogs, and parrots. Robertson died in St. Petersburg in 1854.

The present portrait of Nikolai Alekseevich Stolypin dates from this second trip. Nikolai was born in 1843 to Maria Vasilievna (née Trobetskaya) and Alexey Stolypin, who married in 1839. Maria had grown up in the Imperial court, and was a favorite of the tsar’s family, especially of Grand Duchess Maria Nikolaevna, the eldest daughter of Nicholas I. Already a prominent figure in high society, in 1835, she became a lady-in-waiting to Empress Alexandra. Alexey Stolypin was a Staff Captain of the Life Guards Hussar Regiment, and thanks to his wife’s closeness to the royal family, Stolypin rose in social status, eventually becoming adjutant to Duke Maximilian of Leuchtenberg, who was married to the Grand Duchess Maria. This was to only further intertwine the lives of the Stoylpins with the royal court. Alexey died in 1847, however, and his widow subsequently married Colonel Prince Semyon Mikhailovich Vorontsov, thus making her a princess.

The couple and Nikolai settled in Crimea, in their palace, Alupka, where they frequently hosted lavish gala dinners. Upon Vorontsov’s death in 1882, Maria inherited his vast wealth and estates. She and Nikolai then traveled abroad to her properties in Paris, Geneva, Nice, and Sorrento, and from the mid-1880s, Maria spent most of her time at the Villa Margherita in Florence. Nikolai remained a bachelor, and in 1884, he received the title of Duke of Montelfi from King Umberto I of Italy. The mother and son died within a few years of each other, Maria in 1895 and Nikolai in 1898. In 1900, the property in the Florentine villa was auctioned, though the present portrait was not included in the sale. It is possible that the portrait was left at another one of the family’s properties, and eventually made its way to the United States at an unknown time.

While monumental in size - the present painting is the largest work by Cole to appear at auction in decades - A View of Richmond Hill possesses details and subtleties, along with an unmistakable British bucolic quality not always present in the Portsmouth painter's smaller canvases. The present painting was executed in 1875 and it was exhibited at the Royal Academy. In the present work, Cole depicts figures enjoying the panoramic view from Terrace Walk, highlighted by an elegant woman holding a parasol, with other figures both strolling and seated along the Walk with the Thames winding from the midground to the background behind a line of trees.

Remarkably, the artist had no formal training save for what he learned from his father, the painter George Cole, yet his paintings were exhibited by the Royal Academy - (as was the present painting) - when he was only 20 years old. Lot Essay:
Hailed as one of the “great authorities of his day” by the French art critic Charles Blanc, Guillaume Guillon-Lethière was a painter and draftsman whose work was part of the Neoclassical movement in France, which first emerged in the 1740s and reached popularity from around 1760-1830, a period which nearly coincides exactly with the artist’s life dates. Proponents of Neoclassicism, such as Jacques-Louis David - an artist known to Guillon-Lethiere from his frequent visits to the former’s studio and who would later become Guillon-Lethiere’s rival – focused their efforts on scenes from ancient Greece and Rome and emphasized themes of sacrifice, stoicism, civic duty, and heroism. The style was in stark contrast to, and a repudiation of, the lightness and frivolity associated with Rococo art. 

Brutus Condemning His Sons to Death depicts Lucius Junius Brutus, who led a revolt to overthrow the last Roman king and establish the Roman Republic, witnessing the executions of his sons, Tiberius Junius and Titus Junius, who had sought to restore the Tarquin monarchy. While the French public found the composition to be gruesome, it remains one of Guillon-Lethière’s masterpieces with its emphasis on stoicism, duty, and rule of law over self-interest. Two other examples of the same subject painted by Guillon-Lethiere are located in public collections: the Louvre, Paris, and the Clark Art Institute, Williamstown, Massachusetts, museums which also held the first ever exhibition of the artist’s work in Spring, 2024-Winter, 2025, Guillon-Lethiere, Born in Guadeloupe. The present painting most closely follows the composition in the Louvre, while in the Clark Art Institute version, the executioner is seen at left, holding the severed head of one of Brutus’s sons.

Guillon-Lethière’s story is an interesting one: he was a mixed-race son of a white plantation owner and a freed slave of African descent, and was born in the French colony of Guadeloupe. He became a professor at the École de Beaux-Arts and director of the Académie de France in Rome, as well as serving in an advisory capacity to Lucien Bonaparte, the younger brother of Napoleon, helping him to build an art collection.

Lot Note:
Shields was a Manchester painter, watercolorist, and decorator whose artistic career was determined when he saw the works of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood at the Manchester Art Treasures Exhibition of 1857. He later became a close friend of both Rossetti and Ford Madox Brown, although his work, which is strongly realistic and religious in outlook, perhaps comes closer to Holman Hunt than any other Pre-Raphaelite artist. Although he often worked in watercolor and for many years exhibited at the Royal Watercolour Society, his two most substantial commissions were mural decorations for the Chapel of Eaton Hall, Cheshire, seat of the Dukes of Westminster, and the Chapel of the Ascension, Bayswater Road.

This present oil probably relates to the mural at the Chapel of the Ascension. The chapel was commissioned by Mrs. Russell Gurney, widow of the Recorder of London, in the hope that it would provide a sanctuary for meditation away from the hubbub of nearby Marble Arch. The chapel was designed by Herbert Horne in 1887 and although construction began in 1890, legal disputes ensured that it was not completed until 1910. Shields chose to decorate the interior with the principle scenes of Christ's Life and visited Italy in 1889 to gather material for the sequence. The chapel in consequence carried strong echoes of Giotto's fresco cycles in Assissi and Padua. It was destroyed by enemy action during the Second World War.

Lot Essay:
A British engineer, anthropologist, and Egyptologist, John Shae Perring was born in Boston, Lincolnshire in 1813. In 1836, he left for Egypt, where he worked as an engineer on several projects, including those for Muhammad Ali, ruler of Egypt at the time. One of Perring’s main projects was to conduct a survey of the pyramids of Gizeh; he constructed maps and other records of the monuments there. His work was and continues to be an invaluable contribution to research and scholarship on ancient Egypt. 

Views of Egypt is a fascinating collection of watercolors, prints, and drawings that Perring made to document his sightings. The collection includes two works of opposite views of the Obelisk at Luxor. One of the depictions exposes a large hole in the foreground where the twin obelisk once stood, before Egypt gifted it to France. Today, it stands in the Place de la Concorde in Paris. 

Perring’s Temples of Abu Simbel, Half-Buried and Temple of Kom Ombo, Half-Buried uniquely depict monuments before excavation. The collection also features a representation of the Mammisi of Cleopatra VII and Ptolemy Caesarion in Perring’s Armant (Hermonthis). This monument was later destroyed so that the stone could be used in the construction of a sugar factory. Evidently, Perring’s works immortalize the monuments as they existed in the 1830s. Whether later excavated, moved, or destroyed, his pieces are records of what once was. They are honest historical documents that future Ancient Egyptian scholarship will continue to rely on: rare and reliable evidence of how the landscape of Egyptian ruins has changed.

Lot Essay:
Victor Alfred Paul Vignon grew up in the village of Villers-Cotterêts and spent the majority of his life in towns on the outskirts of Paris. He enjoyed the nostalgia of the countryside, stating “I should like it to be the countryside of the past, far removed from any noise, still filled with the things of yesteryear.” Vignon was best known for his Impressionist paintings, with collectors and art dealers fascinated by his work, with its undoubted Impressionist charm, but also its stylistic diversions from the movement. 

Vignon contributed to four of eight Impressionist exhibitions in the late nineteenth century. As many Impressionists did, he developed an artistic understanding by visiting the Louvre and studying the Old Masters. He worked alongside other painters, notably Camille Pissarro and Paul Cézanne, but his work amalgamates a variety of influences that distinguish him from the other Impressionists. While his work represents the progressiveness of Impressionism and its obsession with light, color, and dynamic brushstrokes, it also is nostalgia embodied, neat and reminiscent of traditional French landscape painting, with a disregard, or perhaps rejection, of modernity. Art critic Claude Roger-Marx, who owned works by Vignon, wrote: “it was your lot to serve as a link between two schools that succeeded one another and fought...to constitute a transition between what was and what will be, between the art of yesterday and the art of tomorrow.”

Other admirers of Vignon’s work include brothers Theo and Vincent van Gough. Theo owned at least one work by the artist, Woman in a Vineyard, which hung in his dining room. Vignon met Vincent through Theo. Vincent dreamt of living with a community of artists at a house in Arles, inspiring his famous painting The Yellow House, and he considered Vignon a potential participant. Unfortunately, the dream was never realized.

Chemin Montant, translating roughly to Ascending Path, is stunningly emblematic of Vignon’s unique style, painted both playfully and tidily. The winding path and high horizon are characteristic of his oeuvre. Many of the artist’s works explore the motif of the path, perhaps a symbol of the human presence in nature, not disruptive, but passively appreciative. The single figure on the left of the composition further represents this. The woman is one with the landscape, her dress reminiscent of the blue mountains behind her.

The work is an ode to the quiet countryside and the people among it, undisturbed by even a hint of city bustle. Roger-Marx described Vignon’s work as ‘tending towards a less immediate art, more inward-looking' and ‘confess[ing] the hatred of noise, of movement... it speaks of communion with nature.’ Above everything, Vignon was interested in the relationship between man and nature. The path invites the viewer to stand on it, welcoming a similar dialogue, seeking harmony in the landscape and in the self.

Lot Note:
The present work dates from Giovanni Boldini’s formative French period in the late 1870s, when he divided his time between Paris and the Normandy coast. It depicts the rocky beach of Étretat, the picturesque seaside town celebrated for its dramatic cliffs and vibrant fishing port, long favored by artists from Courbet to Monet.

Likely painted around 1879, this rare Normandy view closely echoes the larger and more finished composition now in the collection of the Clark Art Institute, Williamstown. It marks a transitional moment in Boldini’s career, preceding his rise to international fame as a portraitist of Belle Époque society. In Étretat, the artist found an ideal setting to experiment with plein-air painting and contemporary coastal subjects, translating the vitality of modern life into swift, luminous brushwork, as evidenced here. Tramonto con Pescatori is among the few securely documented works from this period and demonstrates Boldini’s remarkable command of atmosphere, movement, and light—the glowing sunset in the distance subtly recalling Monet’s Impression, Soleil Levant (1872–1873), by another frequent visitor to Étretat.

Lot Essay:
Agapit Stevens was a Belgian artist best known for his portraits of women, particularly Orientalist scenes of odalisques and other female figures. Stevens was a member of the L’Essor artists’ association, created in 1876, which sought to rebel against the bourgeois, extremely conservative artistic circles in Brussels at the time. The L’Essor motto was “a unique art, one life,” as the group explored the relationship between art and life in their work.  

Gathering Flowers is a portrayal of a young woman carrying, presumably freshly picked, flowers in the forest. Unlike many of Stevens’ other representations of European women, she is not sitting in a luxurious home, adorned with opulent jewelry. She instead is represented in somewhat scandalous attire: the strap of her corset falls off the shoulder with which she leans toward the viewer. There is a sensual nature to the work, somewhat reminiscent of the odalisque tradition that Stevens so often explored. This is underscored by the woman’s direct gaze that seemingly invites the viewer to gather fresh flowers while in her lovely company.

Lot Essay:
Paul Joseph Victor Dargaud was a French artist who created many landscape, genre, and still life paintings, but was most well-known for his scenes of Paris. He was particularly skilled at representing architecture, in which he rendered each structure and building with incredible accuracy, detail, and proportion. Fascinatingly, he created a series of works to demonstrate the various stages of the construction of the Statue of Liberty in Paris.

L’Hotel de Ville de Paris is a stunning depiction of the administrative center of the city. The current building was ordered by King Francis I around 1533 and finished in 1628. Situated along the Seine, L’Hotel de Ville serves as the official mayoral office and hosts the local government. This Italian Renaissance-style building has witnessed numerous momentous occasions, including the arrival of Queen Victoria in Paris in 1855, but it is its own part in history that makes is so fascinating. At the close of the Franco-Prussian War in 1871, a group of protestors from the Paris Commune set fire to L’Hotel de Ville, in objection to France’s surrender. Nothing but the shell of the building remained. It was reconstructed, but larger, maintaining the sixteenth century facade while updating the interior to represent late nineteenth century extravagance, even including a replica of the Hall of Mirrors of the Palace of Versailles. The building’s reconstruction does not try to contrive a sense of pure, untouched Renaissance charm. Rather, the grandiose interior serves as a reminder of what the building has endured.

The present work by Dargaud effectively immortalizes the version of Paris that was right in front of the artist. It considers the transient, ever-shifting nature of the modern cityscape, with its architecture as it exists in a single moment of time, acknowledging the possibility of change. Even the sturdiest, most muscular structures are subject to fire, literal or metaphorical. Permanence is a fragile illusion, but Victor Dargaud’s art comes close.

Lot Essay:
Ready About (Paré à Virer), 1888, is a monumental work by the artist Eugène Vail, who was born in France to a French mother and an American father. At the insistence of his father, he studied at the Stevens Institute of Technology in Hoboken, New Jersey, where he graduated with a degree in mechanical engineering in 1877. After college he joined the National Guard, traveling with a Western expedition led by Captain George Wheeler. At the end of his service, and now free to pursue his true interest, Vail became a student of William Merritt Chase and J. Carroll Beckwith at the Art Students League in New York before returning to France. In Paris, he entered the École des Beaux-Arts in 1882, where he was instructed by Alexandre Cabanel, Raphaël Collin, and Pascal Adolphe Jean Dagnan-Bouveret, the latter the leader of the Naturalist School.

Like many artists of the late 19th century, Vail frequented Pont-Aven and Concarneau in Brittany, but eventually was attracted to Étaples, in Boulogne, along the northern coast of France. With its traditional fishing industry and rustic seafarers, Étaples appealed to both French and foreign painters alike. Vail was drawn to the life of the hardworking sailors, who he accurately depicted engaging in fishing activities, often with a sober palette of cool colors and in enormous formats.

It was here in Étaples that the artist executed Ready About (Paré à Virer), in 1888. Measuring at an impressive 94 x 125 ½ inches, the painting won a third-class gold medal in the Paris Salon of 1888, then in the following year, it won a first-class gold medal at the Paris Exposition Universelle. The composition is close-cropped, as if the viewer is sitting in the bow of the diagonally rocking boat. Two sailors strain to pull a rope in the immediate foreground and are depicted at almost life-sized. In the stern and at an elevated position, the captain powerfully grips the helm as he looks out over the rolling waves that threaten to capsize his vessel. With its uniform use of rectangular strokes, Vail's vigorous brushwork emphasizes the dynamic movement of the image. The overall green-gray tonalities likewise evoke the cold and wet conditions of the rough waters, with only the vivid red flesh of the day’s catch in the boat’s lower right corner to punctuate the chilly atmosphere. Theodore Child wrote about this painting: "very beautiful in color, and amongst the very strongest and best pictures of this kind in the Exhibition." (T. Child, "American Artists at the Paris Exposition." Harper's New Monthly Magazine, September 1889, p. 518)

In 1897, the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, acquired the present work directly from Vail for a sum of $1,000. Vail reportedly instructed the gallery that it should be examined "at some distance, as it was painted with the object of carrying best at about twelve feet." The same year, the Mancini Gallery in Paris welcomed:

Eugène Vail, whose previous successes had long since brought him to the attention of the discerning, who is currently in full development, and it is to a new form of art that he now devotes his fully mature talent. He is an evocative artist. His vigorous and calm colorings give a deep emotion, for this painter translates nature without sentimentality and knows how to convey to the mind of the spectator the feeling and impression that emerge from beings and things. A happy mixture of symbolism and reality, a disturbing evocation of art, such is the work of Eugène Vail, who has managed to imprint on his canvases a conscientious, bold, original individuality, which deserves to capture the attention of the most enlightened art lovers. (L'Intransigeant, December 25, 1897, p. 3)

Lot Essay:
Painted by Montague Dawson, one of the foremost nautical painters of the 20th century, The Flying Clipper “The Cutty Sark” is a dynamic depiction of the clipper as she races back towards England in an attempt to win another of the great Tea Races. The Scottish shipbuilding firm Scott & Linton of Dumbarton was commissioned by Captain John Willis in 1869 to build the ship, whose famous racing career began with her first voyage to China in 1870. The name of the Cutty Sark is taken from one of Robbie Burns’s most famous poems, in which Tam o’Shanter’s beautiful witch dances in her ‘cutty sark,’ or short chemise. In this guise, she formed the figurehead of the new clipper, which can be seen with long hair and chemise flowing in the wind.

Although at first thought to be either unlucky or a failure due to not making the voyage from Shanghai to England in less than a hundred days, she later proved to be one of the fastest ships ever built. One of Cutty Sark’s outstanding voyages was to China in the winter of 1870/71, when she took only 98 days from London to Shanghai. During this voyage she encountered strong gales, snow, thundery squalls, and was also becalmed outside the Manipa Strait. n 1895, the clipper was sold to a firm in Lisbon, and her name changed to Ferreira. Under both names, the clipper was to go on to transport thousands of tons of goods all over the world, with a career often characterized by lucky escapes. The Suez Canal forced it from the tea trade for which it had been built, yet it thrived as a cargo ship bringing Australian wool to the UK. In 1906 it survived a hurricane in Florida which killed 134 people. Then, in 1916, it was laid up for over two years after nearly sinking off the coast of South Africa (however, this meant it avoided the threat of German U-boats).

In 1922, the aging clipper was purchased by Captain Wilfred Dowman of Trevissone, near Plymouth. On its penultimate voyage, the ship had been damaged in a storm and called into Falmouth for repairs, where she was recognized by the captain. 27 years previously, Dowman had been an apprentice on board the sailing ship Hawksdale, when Cutty Sark surged past, leaving a lasting impression on the young man. He re-rigged her to her original sail and spar plan, in the hopes of racing her to Port Jackson. However, in 1936 Dowman died before being able to do so. His widow, Catherine Dowman, then presented the Cutty in 1938 to the Thames Nautical College, in Greenwich, where she was to be used as a training ship for boys seeking careers in the Royal and Merchant Navies.

The outbreak of World War II led to the boys being moved ashore, and the Cutty Sark again began to fall again into disrepair. Eventually, Frank Carr, the determined Director of the National Maritime Museum, in Greenwich, raised funds and interest for the ship’s preservation, and in 1954 she was installed at a dry dock located outside the museum. The sole surviving tea clipper in the world was opened to the public in 1957 by HM The Queen in 1957, where she can still be visited today.
